summary: Lists the requirements that a callout protocol must meet to support remote execution of OPES services, where an edge device hands data to another server for processing. The requirements are meant to help evaluate candidate protocols and guide their design.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3836 is the requirement list for the protocol that OPES uses to talk to a remote callout server. It describes what such a protocol has to do: carry application messages reliably, let a server answer before the whole message has arrived, cope with messages too big to send at once, negotiate what both sides can do, and keep the exchange private.

questions: what is an opes callout protocol
what must a callout protocol do
subtitle: What a protocol must do to let a network device hand application messages to a remote server for processing

tldr.problem: Under the OPES architecture a network device can send the application messages it sees to a remote callout server, which filters, transforms or logs them and sends the result back. Nobody had defined what the protocol between the two must do.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements in three groups: functional, covering transactions, connections, message fragmentation and negotiation; performance, covering the delay the protocol adds; and security, covering authentication, confidentiality and integrity.
tldr.outcome: The requirements are written to evaluate candidate protocols and guide new ones, so a protocol that keeps messages reliable and ordered, can be cut short mid-message, can negotiate capabilities and protects the exchange should satisfy them. The memo defines no protocol itself.

facts.label: Functional requirement areas
facts.value: 13, from reliability to metadata and instructions

facts.label: Transport for reliable delivery
facts.value: A transport with ordered reliability, for example TCP or SCTP

today: RFC 3836 is an Informational memo from August 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a requirement document for the OPES callout protocol, intended to help evaluate candidate protocols and guide the design of new ones, and it defines no protocol of its own.

sections.title: What the Callout Protocol Is For
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services architecture enables cooperative application services between a data provider, a data consumer and zero or more OPES processors. The application services under consideration analyse, and possibly transform, application-level messages exchanged between the data provider and the data consumer.

The execution of such services is governed by a set of rules installed on the OPES processor, and enforcing the rules can trigger the execution of service applications local to that processor. Alternatively, the processor can distribute the responsibility of service execution by communicating and collaborating with one or more remote callout servers. An OPES processor communicates with and invokes services on a callout server by using a callout protocol, and this document presents the requirements for such a protocol. The requirements are divided into three categories, functional, performance and security, and each requirement is presented as one or more statements followed by brief explanatory material.
sections.plainLanguage: In plain terms: the device on the path can ask a specialist server elsewhere to look at each message, and get back either a changed message or a verdict. This memo says what that conversation has to look like.

sections.title: Callout Transactions and Connections
sections.content:
The protocol must provide ordered reliability for the communication between an OPES processor and a callout server, and should also be able to provide unordered reliability. To satisfy that, it should specify that it is used with a transport protocol that provides ordered or unordered reliability at the transport layer, for example TCP or SCTP. It must ensure that congestion avoidance matching the standard of RFC 2914 is applied to all communication between the two, so a congestion-controlled transport such as TCP or SCTP should be used.

It must enable a processor and a callout server to perform callout transactions for the purpose of exchanging partial or complete application-level protocol messages, or modifications of them. The processor must be able to forward a partial or complete application message so that one or more OPES services can process it, and the server must be able to return a modified application message, or the modified parts of one, to the processor. The server must also be able to report the result of the transaction, for example as a status code.

A callout transaction is a message exchange consisting of a callout request and a callout response, and each of those may consist of one or more protocol messages. A request must always contain a partial or complete application message, a response must always indicate the result of the transaction, and a response may contain a modified application message. Transactions are always initiated by a request from the processor and typically terminated by a response from the server, but the protocol must also let either end terminate a transaction before the request or response has been completely received, and that mechanism must ensure that premature termination does not lose application message data. Premature termination is required to support services that finish early, such as content analysis services that may classify a web object after processing just the first few bytes.

The protocol must enable multiple transactions over a callout connection, and must provide a way of associating transactions with connections. A callout connection is a logical application-layer connection between the processor and the server, and it may have parameters associated with it, for example ones controlling the fail-over behaviour of connection endpoints, which may be negotiated between the two. The protocol may multiplex multiple connections over a single transport-layer connection, if a flow control mechanism that guarantees fairness among the multiplexed connections is applied. Connections must always be initiated by the processor, and may be closed by either endpoint provided that doing so does not affect the operation of ongoing transactions on that connection.

The protocol must support asynchronous message exchange, so that request issuance can be separated from response processing, with multiple outstanding requests and a method of correlating responses with requests. It must also enable a callout server to respond to a request before it has received the whole request.

Message segmentation is required in both directions. The processor must be able to forward an application message in a series of smaller fragments and the server must be able to re-assemble them, and the server must be able to return an application message in fragments that the processor re-assembles. Depending on the application protocol on the data path, application messages may be very large, as with audio or video streams, or of unknown size, and in both cases the processor has to start a transaction before it has received the whole message to avoid long delays for the data consumer. So the processor must be able to forward fragments as it receives them, and the server must be able to process and return fragments as it receives them. Segmentation is also required if the protocol provides a flow control mechanism to multiplex multiple connections over one transport connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has to be able to look at a message while it is still arriving, decide early, and hand back a changed version. That means the protocol has to handle pieces of a message in both directions and reassemble them at the other end.

sections.title: Staying Alive and Dealing with More Than One Peer
sections.content:
The protocol must provide a keep-alive mechanism which, if used, would allow both endpoints of a connection to detect a failure of the other endpoint even in the absence of callout transactions. It may specify that keep-alive messages are exchanged over existing callout connections or over a separate connection, and may specify that the use of the mechanism is optional. Detecting a callout server failure may let the processor establish a connection with a stand-by server so that future transactions do not lose application message data, and detecting a processor failure may let the server release resources that would otherwise not be available for transactions with other processors.

The protocol should be NAT-friendly, meaning its operation should not be compromised by the presence of NAT devices in the path between the processor and the server.

The protocol must allow a processor to communicate simultaneously with more than one callout server, because in larger networks OPES services are likely to be hosted by different callout servers, so a processor will likely have to talk to several. It must also allow a callout server to communicate simultaneously with more than one OPES processor, and the design must support a scenario in which several processors use the services of one server.

The protocol should be application protocol agnostic, making no assumptions about the application-layer protocol used on the data path between the data provider and the consumer, and at a minimum it must be compatible with HTTP. The OPES entities on the data path may use different application-layer protocols, including HTTP and RTP, and it would be desirable to use the same callout protocol for any such protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: There has to be a way to notice that the other end has gone, so a stand-by can take over, and the protocol has to cope with several servers and several processors at once. It also has to work when a NAT box sits in between.

sections.title: Negotiating Capabilities and Carrying Metadata
sections.content:
The protocol must support the negotiation of capabilities and callout connection parameters between the processor and the callout server. The two must be able to exchange their capabilities and preferences, and then to engage in a deterministic negotiation process that ends either with the endpoints agreeing on the capabilities and parameters to be used for future connections and transactions, or with a determination that their capabilities are incompatible. The things that could be negotiated include the callout protocol version, fail-over behaviour, the heartbeat rate for keep-alive messages and security related parameters. The protocol must not use negotiation to determine the transport protocol used for connections, though it may specify that a certain application message protocol, such as HTTP or RTP, requires a certain transport protocol.

Connection parameters may also pertain to the characteristics of the OPES services themselves, for example when a connection is associated with specific services: a service-specific parameter may specify which parts of an application message the service needs. Connection parameters must be negotiated per connection and before any transactions are performed over it, while other parameters and capabilities, such as fail-over behaviour, may be negotiated independently of connections. The parties may negotiate over the callout connections themselves, or a separate control connection may be used for the purpose.

The protocol must provide a mechanism for the endpoints of a transaction to include metadata and instructions in the request and the response. The processor must be able to include information about the forwarded application message, for instance to specify the type of message or which parts of it are being forwarded, and the server must be able to include information about the message it returns. The processor must further be able to include an ordered list of one or more uniquely specified OPES services to be performed on the forwarded message in the specified order, though if the protocol associates connections with specific services there may be no need to identify services per transaction.

The protocol must allow the server to indicate to the processor the cacheability of callout responses, so responses may have to carry cache-control instructions, and it must enable the processor to tell the server whether it has kept a local copy of the forwarded message, which lets the server decide whether the message must be returned even if no service changed it. The protocol must also allow processors to comply with the tracing requirements of the OPES architecture, which means the server must be able to convey information about the service operations it performed on the forwarded message.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any work starts, the two ends agree what they can each do and how they should fail over. Along with each request come notes about what the message is, which services should run on it, and whether the answer may be cached.

sections.title: Efficiency
sections.content:
The callout protocol should have minimal latency, and the size and complexity of its headers could be minimised as one way of achieving that. Because callout transactions add latency to the application protocol transactions on the data path, the efficiency of the callout protocol is crucial to the overall performance of the data path. A user waiting on a web page does not wait only for the network to carry the page, but for the callout exchange in the middle of it as well.

The memo's own security considerations section adds nothing further: it simply points at the security requirements set out in the previous section.
sections.plainLanguage: Every callout costs time, and the user is waiting, so the protocol should add as little delay as possible and keep its headers small.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
In the absence of any security mechanisms, sensitive information might be communicated between the OPES processor and the callout server in violation of either endpoint's security and privacy policy, through misconfiguration or deliberate insider attack. By using strong authentication, message encryption and integrity checks, this threat can be minimised to a smaller set of insiders and operator configuration errors. The processor and the callout servers should have enforceable policies that limit the parties they communicate with and determine the protections to use based on the identities of the endpoints and other data such as end user policies, and to enforce those policies they must be able to authenticate the callout protocol endpoints using cryptographic methods.

The parties to the callout protocol must have a sound basis for binding authenticated identities to the protocol endpoints, and must verify that these identities are consistent with their security policies. The protocol must provide for message authentication, confidentiality and integrity between the processor and the server, and it must provide mutual authentication. It should use existing security mechanisms; the callout protocol specification is not required to specify them, but may refer to a lower-level security protocol and discuss how its mechanisms are to be used.

If hop-by-hop encryption is a requirement for the content path, that confidentiality must be extended to the communication between the processor and the server. Although it is recommended that this communication always be encrypted, it may be optional if the processor and the server are co-located in a single administrative domain with strong confidentiality guarantees. To minimise data exposure, the callout protocol must use a different encryption key for each encrypted content stream.

The protocol must operate securely across untrusted domains between the processor and the server: if the communication channels cross outside the organisation responsible for the OPES services, then endpoint authentication and message protection for confidentiality and integrity must be used. Finally, any communication carrying information relevant to privacy policies must protect the data using encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends must prove who they are to each other, and the content must be scrambled on the way, especially when the call leaves the organisation that runs the service. Each encrypted stream gets its own key, so a leak of one does not expose the others.

messages.label: CALLOUT REQUEST
messages.note: Carries a partial or complete application message, and may name the services to run on it.

messages.label: CALLOUT RESPONSE
messages.note: Always states the result of the transaction, and may carry the modified application message.

items.title: Reliability
items.text: Ordered delivery between processor and server, unordered as well if possible

items.title: Congestion avoidance
items.text: The same congestion control the Internet uses elsewhere, so a callout cannot flood the link

items.title: Callout transactions
items.text: A request and a response, either of which may be cut short without losing data

items.title: Callout connections
items.text: Many transactions over one connection, with parameters such as fail-over behaviour

items.title: Asynchronous exchange
items.text: Many requests in flight at once, with responses matched to them

items.title: Segmentation
items.text: Big messages sent in pieces and reassembled at the other end

items.title: Keep-alive
items.text: A way to notice the other end has gone, so a stand-by can take over

items.title: Negotiation
items.text: The two ends agree versions, fail-over behaviour and security parameters before starting
